questions.sub: Primordial Respiratory Diverticulum and Germ Layer Origins
questions.q: From which primary embryonic germ layer does the epithelial lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and pulmonary alveoli originate?
questions.explain: During week 4, the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) evaginates from the ventral wall of the foregut endoderm, giving rise to the epithelial lining of the entire lower respiratory tract, whereas cartilage, smooth muscle, and connective tissue arise from splanchnic mesoderm.

open.q: Which embryonic germ layer gives rise to the epithelial lining of the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli?

questions.sub: Primordial Respiratory Diverticulum and Germ Layer Origins
questions.q: Which embryonic tissue gives rise to the hyaline cartilage rings, smooth muscle, elastic fibers, and visceral pleura of the lower respiratory tract?
questions.explain: As the endodermal respiratory bud grows caudally into the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm, that splanchnic mesoderm differentiates into tracheal/bronchial cartilage, smooth muscle, blood vessels, connective tissue, and the visceral pleura (whereas somatic mesoderm forms the parietal pleura).

open.q: From which specific subdivision of mesoderm do the tracheal cartilages, bronchial smooth muscle, and visceral pleura develop?

questions.sub: Primordial Respiratory Diverticulum and Germ Layer Origins
questions.q: At approximately which post-fertilization week does the laryngotracheal groove and respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) first appear on the ventral wall of the foregut?
questions.explain: Around day 26–28 (week 4), retinoic acid signaling induces TBX4 expression in foregut mesoderm, triggering the laryngotracheal groove and ventral respiratory diverticulum immediately caudal to the fourth pharyngeal pouch.

open.q: During which embryonic week does the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) first evaginate from the foregut?

questions.q: Which longitudinal partition forms by fusion of the bilateral tracheoesophageal folds to separate the ventral laryngotracheal tube from the dorsal esophagus?
questions.explain: Longitudinal ridges (tracheoesophageal folds) invaginate from the lateral walls of the foregut and fuse in the midline to create the tracheoesophageal septum, dividing the foregut into a ventral respiratory primordium and a dorsal esophagus.

open.q: Name the midline partition formed by fusion of the tracheoesophageal folds that divides the foregut into the trachea and esophagus.

questions.q: A newborn develops copious frothy salivation, choking, cyanosis upon the first feeding, inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach, and marked abdominal distension with air visible in the stomach on chest-abdominal X-ray. Which anatomical variant accounts for ~85–90% of tracheoesophageal anomalies?
options: Proximal esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
Isolated H-type tracheoesophageal fistula without atresia
Distal esophageal atresia with a proximal tracheoesophageal fistula
Isolated esophageal atresia without any fistula
questions.explain: Posterior deviation of the tracheoesophageal septum produces proximal blind-ending esophageal atresia (causing drooling, choking, and coiled NG tube) combined with a fistula connecting the lower esophagus to the trachea near the carina (allowing inspired air to distend the stomach and gastric acid to reflux into the lungs).

open.q: In the most common form (~85–90%) of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula, which segment of the esophagus communicates with the trachea?

questions.q: Why is maternal polyhydramnios frequently detected on prenatal ultrasound when a fetus has esophageal atresia?
options: Upper gastrointestinal obstruction prevents the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid into the gut for absorption
The blind esophageal pouch secretes excessive fluid
The tracheoesophageal fistula pumps amniotic fluid out of the lungs
questions.explain: In utero, the fetus swallows amniotic fluid which is absorbed in the small intestine and cleared across the placenta; esophageal atresia blocks swallowed fluid from reaching the absorptive gut, leading to polyhydramnios.

open.q: What amniotic fluid volume abnormality is classically seen prenatally in pregnancies complicated by fetal esophageal atresia?

questions.q: From which pharyngeal arches do the cartilages and intrinsic striated muscles of the larynx develop?
questions.explain: Laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) arise from neural crest/mesenchyme of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6, and intrinsic laryngeal muscles are innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve (arch 4) and recurrent laryngeal nerve (arch 6) of CN X.

open.q: Which two pharyngeal arches give rise to the cartilages and intrinsic muscles of the larynx?

questions.q: During weeks 8 to 10, rapid proliferation of laryngeal epithelium temporarily obliterates the laryngeal lumen before recanalization occurs. Incomplete recanalization of the laryngeal lumen results in:
options: Congenital laryngeal web or laryngeal atresia
questions.explain: Temporary epithelial proliferation closes the laryngeal inlet during weeks 8–10 and normally recanalizes by week 10 (forming the laryngeal ventricles and vocal folds); partial failure produces a membranous laryngeal web causing neonatal stridor and weak cry.

open.q: Incomplete recanalization of the embryonic laryngeal lumen around week 10 causes what congenital airway anomaly?

questions.sub: Bronchial Tree and Lung Bud Branching
questions.q: How do the right and left primary bronchial buds differ anatomically from the outset during week 5 of embryonic development?
options: The right primary bronchial bud is slightly larger and oriented more vertically than the left primary bronchial bud
The left primary bronchial bud is wider and strictly vertical
The right lung forms two secondary lobar bronchi while the left forms three
Only the right bronchial bud develops cartilage
questions.explain: From week 5 onward, the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical (explaining why aspirated foreign bodies preferentially enter the right bronchial tree), and divides into 3 secondary (lobar) bronchi on the right versus 2 on the left.

open.q: How many secondary (lobar) bronchi form on the right side versus the left side during week 5?
accept: 3 on the right and 2 on the left

questions.sub: Bronchial Tree and Lung Bud Branching
questions.q: How many bronchopulmonary segments (supplied by tertiary/segmental bronchi) normally develop in each lung by week 7?
options: 10 bronchopulmonary segments in the right lung and 8 to 9 in the left lung
5 in the right lung and 5 in the left lung
3 in the right lung and 2 in the left lung
questions.explain: Each secondary lobar bronchus branches dichotomously into tertiary (segmental) bronchi—10 in the right lung and 8–9 in the left lung—each accompanied by a branch of the pulmonary artery and surrounded by connective tissue septa.

open.q: State the normal number of bronchopulmonary segments in the adult right lung.

questions.sub: Bronchial Tree and Lung Bud Branching
questions.q: Which signaling molecule secreted by the distal splanchnic mesenchyme acts on FGFR2b receptors in the endodermal lung bud tips to stimulate branching morphogenesis?
questions.explain: Epithelial-mesenchymal interactions drive branching morphogenesis: splanchnic mesenchyme secretes FGF10 to promote bud outgrowth and bifurcation, while bud tips express Sonic hedgehog (SHH) and BMP4 to locally downregulate FGF10 at the cleft and split the bud.

open.q: Name the mesenchymal fibroblast growth factor that induces outgrowth and dichotomous branching of endodermal lung buds.

questions.q: What is the correct chronological order of the four histological stages of prenatal lung maturation (plus the postnatal stage)?
options: Embryonic → Pseudoglandular → Canalicular → Terminal sac (saccular) → Alveolar
questions.explain: Lung maturation progresses through five overlapping stages: Embryonic (weeks 4–7), Pseudoglandular (weeks 5–17), Canalicular (weeks 16–25), Terminal sac/Saccular (weeks 24–birth), and Alveolar (late fetal period through ~8 years postnatally).

open.q: List the four prenatal histological stages of lung development in chronological order.

questions.q: During the pseudoglandular stage (weeks 5 to 17), why is survival of a fetus born during this period impossible even with mechanical ventilation?
options: Only conducting airways to terminal bronchioles have formed; gas-exchanging units and an effective blood-air barrier are absent
The trachea has not separated from the oesophagus
questions.explain: In the pseudoglandular stage, the developing lung resembles an exocrine tubuloacinar gland on histology; all conducting airways down to terminal bronchioles form, but no gas-exchanging acinar structures or capillaries are apposed to the airway epithelium.

open.q: Which generation of conducting airways represents the distal limit of bronchial branching at the end of the pseudoglandular stage (week 17)?

questions.q: Which key developmental milestones occur during the canalicular stage of lung maturation (weeks 16 to 25)?
options: Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts form, capillaries approach the epithelium, and type I/II pneumocytes differentiate
The laryngotracheal diverticulum first buds from the foregut
questions.explain: During the canalicular stage (weeks 16–25), airway lumina enlarge, respiratory bronchioles and primitive alveolar ducts form, capillaries grow closely adjacent to cuboidal epithelium, and type II pneumocytes begin secreting surfactant around weeks 22–24, making survival possible at the end of this stage.

open.q: Around which gestational weeks during the late canalicular stage do type II pneumocytes begin producing pulmonary surfactant?

questions.q: During the terminal sac (saccular) stage (week 24 to birth), thin-walled terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) become closely apposed to capillaries to establish the blood-air barrier. Which epithelial cell type flattens to line ~95% of the alveolar surface area for gas exchange?
options: Type I alveolar epithelial cells (type I pneumocytes)
Type II alveolar epithelial cells (type II pneumocytes)
questions.explain: Type I pneumocytes differentiate from type II pneumocytes and become extremely attenuated squamous cells (~0.1 um thick) covering ~95% of the alveolar surface and sharing a fused basal lamina with capillary endothelial cells.

open.q: Which alveolar epithelial cell type forms the thin squamous lining covering ~95% of the alveolar surface for gas diffusion?

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of mature adult alveoli (300–400 million) are formed AFTER birth during the alveolar stage (extending from ~36 weeks gestation up to 8 years of age)?
questions.explain: At full-term birth, only about 20–50 million primitive alveoli (5–15% of the adult total) are present; ~85–95% of mature alveoli develop postnatally via secondary septation of saccules over the first 3 to 8 years of life.

open.q: Up to approximately what postnatal age in years does the alveolar stage of lung development continue to generate new alveoli via secondary septation?

questions.sub: Surfactant and Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.q: What is the primary phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant secreted by type II pneumocytes that lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents end-expiratory atelectasis?
questions.explain: Pulmonary surfactant is a lipid-protein mixture (~90% lipid, ~10% surfactant proteins SP-A, B, C, D) whose major surface-active phospholipid is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC / lecithin), reducing alveolar surface tension according to the Law of Laplace (P = 2T/r).

open.q: Name the principal phospholipid in pulmonary surfactant responsible for lowering alveolar surface tension.

questions.sub: Surfactant and Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.q: Which amniotic fluid biochemical test ratio rises sharply around week 34 to 35 of gestation and indicates fetal lung maturity when greater than 2.0?
questions.explain: Sphingomyelin levels in amniotic fluid remain relatively constant throughout pregnancy, whereas lecithin (DPPC) surges after week 32–34; an L/S ratio ≥ 2.0 (along with presence of phosphatidylglycerol) reliably predicts mature surfactant production.

open.q: What minimum amniotic fluid lecithin-to-sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio indicates mature fetal pulmonary surfactant production?

questions.sub: Surfactant and Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.q: A preterm male infant born at 29 weeks gestation to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes develops tachypnea, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, expiratory grunting, and diffuse 'ground-glass' reticulogranular infiltrates with air bronchograms on chest X-ray (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome). Why does maternal diabetes increase RDS risk even at later gestational ages?
options: Fetal hyperinsulinemia inhibits glucocorticoid-induced surfactant synthesis by type II pneumocytes
Maternal insulin destroys type I pneumocytes directly
Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.explain: Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia; elevated fetal insulin antagonizes cortisol stimulation of type II pneumocytes, delaying DPPC/surfactant synthesis and predisposing to hyaline membrane disease (RDS).

open.q: Which medication is administered antenatally to mothers in preterm labor (24–34 weeks) to accelerate fetal type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production?

questions.sub: Fetal Breathing Movements and Lung Liquid Clearance
questions.q: How is the fetal lung liquid that fills the developing airways during gestation cleared at the time of birth?
options: Labour-related catecholamines promote epithelial sodium absorption; fluid is then cleared by pulmonary capillaries and lymphatics
Fetal lung liquid is excreted entirely through the umbilical arteries
Fluid is swallowed through the ductus arteriosus
Fluid evaporates across the fetal skin
questions.explain: Before birth, fetal lung epithelium secretes Cl- and fluid to distend the airways; labor surges of epinephrine and glucocorticoids switch alveolar epithelium from Cl- secretion to Na+ absorption via ENaC channels, drawing water into the interstitium for rapid lymphatic and capillary clearance.

open.q: What transient neonatal respiratory condition occurs when delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid—commonly after elective cesarean section without labor—causes mild tachypnea resolving within 24–72 hours?

questions.q: Which embryonic membranes grow medially to close the pericardioperitoneal canals during week 7 and separate the pleural cavities from the peritoneal cavity?
questions.explain: During weeks 5–7, the paired pleuroperitoneal membranes grow ventromedially to fuse with the septum transversum and dorsal mesentery of the esophagus, sealing off the pleural cavities from the peritoneal cavity.

open.q: Name the paired embryonic membranes that fuse with the septum transversum and esophageal mesentery to close the pericardioperitoneal canals.

questions.q: From which four embryonic structures does the definitive human diaphragm develop?
options: Septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and muscular ingrowth from body walls
Amnion, chorion, yolk sac and allantois
questions.explain: The diaphragm is a composite structure formed by: (1) septum transversum (central tendon), (2) pleuroperitoneal membranes, (3) dorsal mesentery of the esophagus (crura), and (4) somatic mesoderm/myoblasts from cervical somites C3–C5 via the lateral body walls (peripheral musculature).

open.q: Which embryonic component of the diaphragm gives rise to its adult central tendon?

questions.q: Why is the adult diaphragm innervated by the phrenic nerves originating from cervical spinal segments C3, C4, and C5 despite its final anatomical position at the thoracoabdominal junction?
options: The diaphragm originates in the cervical region and descends during development, retaining C3–C5 phrenic innervation
The vagus nerve degenerates in the thorax
Lumbar spinal nerves fail to reach the abdomen
The phrenic nerve grows upward from the sacrum
questions.explain: In week 4, the septum transversum lies opposite cervical somites C3–C5 and receives myoblasts and motor axons (phrenic nerves) from C3–C5; differential growth of the dorsal body wall shifts the diaphragm caudally to L1 while lengthening the phrenic nerves ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive').

open.q: Which cervical spinal cord segments supply motor innervation to the diaphragm via the phrenic nerve?

questions.q: A full-term newborn presents immediately after birth with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen, bowel sounds auscultated in the left hemithorax, and mediastinal shift to the right (congenital diaphragmatic hernia). Failure of closure of which embryonic structure most commonly causes this posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect?
questions.explain: Posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek hernia, ~85% left-sided because the left pleuroperitoneal canal closes later than the right and lacks the protective liver) allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax, compressing the developing lungs and causing lethal pulmonary hypoplasia.

open.q: On which side (left or right) do ~85% of posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic (Bochdalek) hernias occur, and what is the primary cause of neonatal mortality in this condition?

questions.q: Which embryonic folds divide the thoracic cavity into a central pericardial cavity and two lateral pleural cavities, containing the phrenic nerves and common cardinal veins within their substance?
questions.explain: As the lung buds expand laterally into the body wall, they split off the pleuropericardial folds containing the common cardinal veins and phrenic nerves; these folds fuse in the midline to form the fibrous pericardium, explaining why the adult phrenic nerves course along the fibrous pericardium.

open.q: Which adult thoracic structure is derived from the fused pleuropericardial membranes and carries the phrenic nerves along its lateral surfaces?

questions.q: A discrete, non-functioning mass of embryonic lung tissue that lacks normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree and receives an anomalous systemic arterial blood supply directly from the thoracic or abdominal aorta is known as:
questions.explain: Bronchopulmonary sequestration arises from an accessory lung bud caudal to the normal lung bud that fails to connect to the bronchial tree and is perfused by an aberrant systemic artery arising directly from the aorta.

open.q: From which major systemic artery does a bronchopulmonary sequestration characteristically receive its arterial blood supply?

questions.q: A blind-ending, fluid- or mucus-filled cyst lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium with cartilage and smooth muscle in its wall—usually located in the middle mediastinum near the carina—results from abnormal budding of the foregut and is called a:
questions.explain: Bronchogenic cysts represent abnormal ventral foregut budding during tracheobronchial branching; they are lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium with hyaline cartilage plates in their wall and commonly lie near the tracheal bifurcation (carina).

open.q: Name the congenital mediastinal cyst lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium and containing wall cartilage that arises from abnormal foregut budding.

questions.q: Persistence of the embryonic oronasal membrane fails to establish continuity between the nasal cavities and the nasopharynx, resulting in a newborn with cyclical cyanosis that worsens during feeding and improves when crying. What is this condition?
questions.explain: Normally, the oronasal membrane ruptures around week 6 to form the primitive choanae; failure to rupture causes congenital choanal atresia (associated with CHARGE syndrome), presenting with cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying in obligate nose-breathing neonates.

open.q: Failure of rupture of which embryonic membrane during week 6 results in congenital choanal atresia?

questions.q: Why does severe, prolonged oligohydramnios (such as in Potter sequence from bilateral renal agenesis) lead to fatal neonatal pulmonary hypoplasia?
options: Thoracic compression and loss of normal lung-fluid distending pressure impair airway branching and alveolar growth
Oligohydramnios causes premature closure of the foramen ovale
The trachea fails to form cartilage rings
questions.explain: Adequate amniotic fluid volume prevents chest wall compression and maintains the positive transpulmonary fluid pressure gradient essential for mechanotransduction-driven lung growth during the canalicular and saccular stages.

open.q: Name the life-threatening developmental lung defect caused by external thoracic compression in Potter sequence or congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.sub: Fetal Breathing Movements and Lung Liquid Clearance
questions.q: What is the physiological role of fetal breathing movements (FBMs), which begin before birth and are detectable on prenatal ultrasound?
options: Fetal breathing movements mechanically stretch the developing lungs and help mature respiratory muscles
They oxygenate fetal blood directly from amniotic fluid
They remove fetal carbon dioxide into the amniotic sac
They prevent closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.explain: Gas exchange in utero occurs exclusively across the placenta; intermittent fetal breathing movements aspirate small amounts of amniotic fluid into the upper airways, providing mechanical stretch stimuli essential for lung parenchymal growth and neuromuscular maturation of the diaphragm and intercostals.

open.q: Do fetal breathing movements contribute to fetal oxygenation in utero, or is their primary function to stimulate lung growth and condition respiratory muscles?
accept: stimulate lung growth and condition respiratory muscles
lung growth and respiratory muscle conditioning
they do not oxygenate the fetus; they promote lung growth and muscle conditioning
